newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian editors appeal to Yeltsin on press freedom.
newsitem.headline: Russian editors appeal to Yeltsin on press freedom.

text.p: Russian newspapers published an open letter from editors to President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday, urging him to come to the defence of media freedoms in two disputes.

The letter, signed by 13 editors, the head of the Russian journalists union and a group which defends freedom of speech, expressed fear of what they called attempts to force editorial policy changes at Izvestia and Komsomolskaya Pravda newspapers.

"Dear Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin). We consider that the president should intervene in this situation," they said in the letter, published by Izvestia, Nezavisimaya Gazeta and Vechernyaya Moskva dailies.
Izvestia is under fire after making relentless attacks on Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and reprinting an article from a French newspaper on the premier's alleged earnings.

Izvestia journalists says an oil company which is its major shareholder has criticised the newspaper for reprinting the article and say it wants to change editorial personnel and policy. The oil company denies it wants to make such changes.
Komsomolskaya Pravda journalists also say they fear shareholders are trying to influence editorial policy.
Behind the dispute are concerns that a small circle of press barons and powerful financial groups are using their stakes in newspapers and television channels to exert political influence.
The debate over press freedom intensified last week when the communist-dominated lower house of parliament set strict limits on television coverage of its sessions.
Yeltsin said earlier this month that the independence of the media was one of the biggest gains of democratic Russia and that he would protect it.
A government spokesmen echoed his views last week, but also criticised a host of publications for printing stories which he said were incorrect.
